entities.name: Adult Self-Report Scale Screener
aliases: مقياس اضطراب فرط الحركة وتشتت الانتباه للبالغين
entities.description: A self-screening questionnaire developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) to help adults aged 18 or older recognize the signs and symptoms of adult ADHD. It is a symptoms checklist and serves as a starting point, not a formal diagnostic tool.

entities.name: Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test
entities.description: The world's most widely used alcohol screening instrument, developed by the World Health Organization in 1989. It is designed to screen for unhealthy alcohol use, including risky or hazardous consumption, alcohol use disorders, and alcohol dependence.

entities.name: CAGE Questions for Alcohol Use
entities.description: A brief, 4-question screening tool used to detect excessive drinking and potential alcoholism. It is less effective in recognizing less severe, non-dependent drinking disorders compared to the AUDIT.

entities.name: General Anxiety Disorder-7
entities.description: A 7-question self-report scale developed by Dr. Robert L. Spitzer to measure the severity of generalized anxiety disorder symptoms.

entities.name: Patient Health Questionnaire-9
entities.description: A 9-question self-report instrument developed by Dr. Kurt Kroenke used to objectify the degree and severity of depression symptoms.

entities.name: PTSD Checklist for DSM-5
aliases: مقياس كرب ما بعد الصدمة PCL-5
entities.description: A 20-item self-report questionnaire developed by the VA's National Center for PTSD to assess the 20 DSM-5 symptoms of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder. Used for screening, provisional diagnosis, and monitoring symptom changes during and after treatment.

entities.name: Rome IV Diagnostic Criteria for Functional Constipation
entities.description: The official clinical diagnostic criteria used to identify functional constipation in patients with symptoms lasting for at least 3 months, while ruling out secondary causes.

entities.name: Rosenberg Self Esteem Scale
entities.description: A 10-item self-report scale developed in the 1960s by Morris Rosenberg to measure general self-esteem. It is the most widely used measure of self-esteem in psychological research but is non-diagnostic.

entities.name: Self-Concept
entities.description: The overall cognitive belief, evaluation, or perception an individual holds about themselves, including their attributes, social roles, traits, and separate existence.

entities.name: Self-Compassion
entities.description: A psychological construct developed by Dr. Kristin Neff that involves offering oneself the same warmth, care, and understanding shown to a close friend in times of struggle, imperfection, or failure.

entities.name: Big Five Personality Model
entities.description: The most widely accepted and scientifically validated model of personality traits in academic psychology. It summarizes personality differences along five independent dimensions: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism.

entities.name: Attachment Styles in Adult Relationships
entities.description: The psychological theory originated by John Bowlby in the 1950s stating that the bond formed with primary caregivers in childhood creates a permanent cognitive template and set of rules for adult intimate, social, and professional relationships.

entities.name: Locus of Control Theory
entities.description: A cognitive factor within Julian Rotter's social learning theory of personality (1954/1966) representing the generalized expectancy of whether life outcomes are driven by one's own actions (internal) or by external forces like fate, luck, and others (external).

entities.name: Self-Talk & Inner Critic
entities.description: The natural, ongoing internal monologue people use to frame their lives, influence their emotions, and regulate their responses to daily events. It can be constructive (positive) or destructive (negative/rumination).

entities.name: Radical Acceptance
entities.description: A therapeutic concept (incorporated in DBT by Marsha Linehan and popularized by Tara Brach) that describes the complete, heart-centered, and somatic embrace of reality and facts as they are, without judgment, resistance, or attempts to fight what is outside of one's control.

facts.context: DSM-5 Assessment for adults aged 17 and older
facts.conditions: Symptoms must have been present since before age 12, persist for at least 6 months, and not be better explained by another condition

facts.conditions: Based on data from a multinational WHO collaborative study

facts.subject: AUDIT
facts.value: Approximately 40 languages
facts.conditions: None

facts.subject: CAGE Questions
facts.value: 4 items: Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener
facts.conditions: None

facts.subject: CAGE Questions
facts.value: Yes = 1 point, No = 0 points; total ranges from 0 to 4
facts.conditions: A score of 0 indicates screening negative
facts.exceptions: If a clinician suspects the patient is minimizing use, qualitative questions should be asked

facts.subject: CAGE
facts.value: Less severe (non-dependent) drinking disorders
facts.context: Clinical efficacy compared to the AUDIT
facts.conditions: In settings where time allows, incorporating AUDIT is recommended to identify a wider spectrum

facts.subject: GAD-7
facts.value: Dr. Robert L. Spitzer
facts.conditions: None

facts.subject: GAD-7 Scale
facts.value: 5-9 (Mild - Monitor), 10-14 (Moderate - Possible clinically significant condition), >15 (Severe - Active treatment probably warranted)
facts.conditions: Cutoff of 10 or more warrants further assessment (referral and clinical diagnostic interview)
facts.exceptions: Cutoff score of 8 may be used for optimal sensitivity/specificity in Panic Disorder, Social Phobia, and PTSD

facts.subject: Before diagnosing an anxiety disorder
facts.value: Ruling out medical causes (e.g., EKG for arrhythmias, TSH for thyroid disease)
facts.conditions: None

facts.subject: PHQ-9
facts.value: Dr. Kurt Kroenke
facts.conditions: None

facts.subject: PHQ-9 Scale
facts.value: 0-4 (Minimal/None), 5-9 (Mild), 10-14 (Moderate), 15-19 (Moderately Severe), 20-27 (Severe)
facts.conditions: Scores of 15 or higher warrant active treatment with psychotherapy, medications, or a combination
facts.exceptions: Bipolar disorder, normal bereavement, and medical disorders causing depression must be ruled out

facts.subject: PHQ-9 Item 9
facts.value: Thoughts of being better off dead or of hurting oneself
facts.conditions: If positive, clinicians must perform a comprehensive suicide risk assessment

facts.subject: PCL-5 Scale
facts.value: 3 formats: 1) Without Criterion A, 2) With a brief Criterion A, 3) With the revised LEC-5 and extended Criterion A
facts.conditions: Takes approximately 5-10 minutes

facts.subject: PCL-5 provisional PTSD diagnosis
facts.value: Treating item ratings of 2 (Moderately) or higher as symptoms endorsed, requiring: 1 B item, 1 C item, 2 D items, 2 E items
facts.conditions: DSM-5 diagnostic rules applied to the 20 items
facts.exceptions: Provisional only; clinical interview (CAPS-5) is the gold standard

facts.subject: PCL-5 probable PTSD cutoff score
facts.value: Between 31 and 33
facts.conditions: Varies by population and screening purpose; lower cutoff maximizes detection, higher minimizes false positives

facts.subject: PCL-5 clinically meaningful change
facts.value: A change of 10 points (indicator of treatment response); or PCL-5 < 28 (indicator of clinically significant change)
facts.conditions: Change compared to baseline scores
facts.exceptions: Based on a study by Marx et al. (2022)

facts.subject: Rome IV Functional Constipation Criteria
facts.value: Symptoms for at least the last 3 months, with symptom onset at least 6 months prior, and ruling out secondary causes
facts.conditions: Secondary causes such as mechanical obstruction, systemic illness, or medications must not be suspected

facts.subject: Rome IV Constipation Alarm Features
facts.value: GI bleeding, unexplained iron deficiency anemia, unintentional weight loss, palpable abdominal mass/lymphadenopathy, family history of colon cancer, onset age >= 50, sudden change in bowel habits
facts.conditions: If any alarm features are present, clinical evaluation for other diagnoses is mandatory

facts.subject: Rome IV Bristol Stool Form Scale
facts.value: Form 1 or 2 of the Bristol Stool Form Scale for more than 1/4 (25%) of defecations
facts.conditions: Must also meet clinical criteria like straining, lumpy/hard stools, sensation of incomplete evacuation, or manual maneuvers for >25% of bowel movements

facts.subject: Self-Concept Definition (Baumeister 1999)
facts.value: The individual's belief about himself or herself, including the person's attributes and who and what the self is
facts.conditions: Forms through experiences, interactions, and reflection

facts.subject: Existential Self Development
facts.value: Around two to three months of age
facts.conditions: Arises due to the infant's physical relationship and feedback loop with the world

facts.subject: Infant Mirror Self-Recognition (Amsterdam 1972)
facts.value: Gradually across the second year of life
facts.conditions: 6-12 months: see reflection as playmate; 14 months: embarrassed/self-conscious reactions; 20-24 months: rouge mark-directed touching in 65% of infants

facts.subject: Mirror Self-Recognition Test
facts.value: Culturally universal
facts.conditions: Cebioğlu & Broesch (2021) showed 68% of Canadian urban toddlers pass vs 7% of rural Ni-Vanuatu toddlers, predicted by mother's imitation parenting style
facts.exceptions: Does not mean absence of self-awareness; rather indicates culture-specific individuation style

facts.subject: Psychological Self
facts.value: Around 3.5 to 4 years of age
facts.conditions: Grants understanding that there is an invisible, thinking self inside the head that others cannot see

facts.subject: Theory of Mind false-belief representation
facts.value: Around 4 to 6 years of age
facts.conditions: Verified by Wimmer and Perner (1983); 3-4 year olds fail, predicting Maxi looks where chocolate really is, while older children pass
facts.exceptions: Modest effect size in better-controlled recent meta-analyses (Barone et al., 2019)

facts.subject: Categorical Self face categorisation
facts.value: 9 months of age
facts.conditions: Infants categorize and recognize faces of their own racial group more easily than other groups

facts.subject: Twenty Statements Test (Kuhn 1960)
facts.value: Self-image along dimensions of social roles and personality traits
facts.conditions: Younger people describe themselves more in terms of personal traits; older people defined more by social roles
facts.exceptions: Kuhn found 7-year-olds gave an average of 5 role-related answers, compared to 10 for undergraduates

facts.subject: Self-Esteem rapid shifts (Morse & Gergen 1970)
facts.value: Rising with 'Mr. Dirty' and falling with 'Mr. Clean'
facts.conditions: Participants waiting for a job interview with a smart vs slovenly confederate

facts.subject: Perseverance Effect (Miller & Ross 1975)
facts.value: People maintain socially desirable self-beliefs even when experimenters present contrary evidence
facts.conditions: Does not always apply to those with very low self-esteem, who may selectively hold only negative self-beliefs

facts.subject: Best Possible Self task (Booth et al. 2025)
facts.value: Positive expectancy and mood directly, and decreases anxiety symptom severity indirectly
facts.conditions: None

facts.subject: Self-Compassion elements
facts.value: 3 components: 1) Self-kindness vs. Self-judgment, 2) Common humanity vs. Isolation, 3) Mindfulness vs. Over-identification
facts.conditions: Requires noticing suffering without pity or over-identification

facts.subject: Fierce Self-Compassion
facts.value: Protecting, providing for, and motivating oneself, drawing boundaries, and standing tall to say no
facts.conditions: Acts in the world to alleviate suffering; contrasted with Yin/Tender self-compassion which involves soothe/accepting
facts.exceptions: Metaphor of Momma Bear protecting her cubs vs parental soothing

facts.subject: Self-Compassion vs Self-Esteem
facts.value: Self-esteem is contingent on success, comparison, and social approval, whereas self-compassion is stable and accepts human flaws
facts.conditions: Self-esteem requires feeling special and above average

facts.subject: Big Five OCEAN Traits
facts.value: Distinct and independent of one another
facts.conditions: A high score in one trait does not predict high or low scores in any of the other four traits

facts.subject: Locus of Control score shift
facts.value: Steady generational shift toward externality in US children and college students from 1960 to 2002
facts.context: Twenge, Zhang, and Im (2004) cross-temporal meta-analysis
facts.conditions: Calculated a shift of roughly 0.80 standard deviations, with average 2002 students scoring more external than 80% of 1960s students

facts.subject: Locus of Control cultural variance
facts.value: The link between an external locus of control and psychological symptoms is significantly stronger in individualist regions compared to collectivist ones
facts.context: Cheng et al. (2013) meta-analysis of 18 cultural regions
facts.conditions: None

facts.conditions: Refer to oneself in the third person (he/she, or by name) rather than the first person (I/me)

facts.subject: Radical Acceptance
facts.value: Pain from transforming into suffering
facts.conditions: Pain is inevitable (nature's signal); suffering is created by fighting, denying, or resisting reality
facts.exceptions: Does not mean approval, passive resignation, or giving up on change

facts.subject: Jungian Shadow/Shadow integration

documents.title: The Story of the Dandelion in Radical Acceptance
documents.content: A story cited on Reddit r/emotionalintelligence: A man bought a new house and tried to grow a beautiful lawn but dandelions kept appearing. He tried endlessly to get rid of them, but they returned year after year. Frustrated, he wrote to the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) for advice. After months, their response arrived: 'Dear Sir, We have considered your inquiry carefully and consulted all our experts... Sir, our recommendation is this: learn to cherish this dandelion.' Radical acceptance involves learning to cherish the dandelions of reality—those unchangeable facts of life that we spend wasteful energy trying to eliminate.

documents.title: The Buddhist Metaphor of the Two Arrows
documents.content: In Buddhist philosophy (recalled on Reddit), life experiences are described through 'two arrows'. The first arrow is the primary pain—the physical or emotional event itself (which is natural, inevitable, and cannot be avoided). The second arrow is suffering—our cognitive resistance, anger, and rejection of the first arrow. Radical Acceptance represents refusing to fire the second arrow, thereby feeling the clean, primary pain without escalating it into agonizing, dirty suffering.

documents.title: CPTSD Perspective on Affirmations vs 'Negative Bridging'
documents.content: On the CPTSD Reddit community, members discuss the struggle with positive affirmations. Direct positive mirror statements ('I am worthy of love') often trigger visceral somatic pain, crying, or feelings of falseness because they conflict too heavily with entrenched toxic shame or core wounds. The consensus recommendation is to practice 'Negative/Neutral Bridging statements' ('I am not entirely gross', 'I am not completely unlovable', 'I am just a person who is trying') which are highly realistic, easier for a damaged cognitive system to accept, and act as a ladder before progressing to positive affirmations.

terms.definition: The most fundamental aspect of the self-concept; the basic cognitive understanding that one exists as a separate, distinct entity from others, with awareness of self-constancy over time and space.
The aspect of the self-concept where the individual defines themselves through objective properties and memberships in social categories (such as age, gender, size, or traits).
The understanding that one possesses a private, invisible, internal thinking and knowing self inside their head that other people cannot directly see.
A state of psychological well-being defined by Carl Rogers where there is consistency, similarity, or match between an individual's real self-image and their ideal self.
The state of mismatch, discrepancy, or inconsistency between an individual's ideal self-concept and their actual life experiences or current self-image.
The gentle, accepting face of self-compassion focused on 'being with' ourselves, soothing our pain, comforting ourselves, and realizing we are not alone.

The powerful, active face of self-compassion focused on 'acting in the world' to alleviate suffering, which involves protecting, providing for, and motivating oneself, drawing boundaries, and saying no.
The belief that one's own efforts, choices, decisions, and actions directly determine and shape the outcomes of their life.
The belief that life outcomes are determined by external factors beyond one's personal control, such as fate, luck, chance, or the actions of powerful others.

The repetitive, circular, and negative process of replaying upsetting, negative, or embarrassing thoughts, memories, or events over and over in one's head, which increases vulnerability to depression and anxiety.

A synthesis of Islamic spiritual concept and psychological acceptance defined by Dr. Mohamed Naji Atiah as completely accepting reality when powerless, delegating outcomes to God, and choosing peace over complaining.
